Network hardware, cables, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth

The cloud and the Internet of Things
intro: Find out what really happens when you send a message, open a website or download a game: the hardware, layouts, addresses and rules that make networks and the internet work.

pages.spec: Explain what a network is, why computers are networked, and the difference between a LAN and a WAN
pages.summary: A network is two or more devices connected so they can share data and resources. A LAN covers a small area like a school; a WAN covers a large area and the internet is the biggest WAN of all.

diagram.title: Stand-alone vs networked
diagram.caption: What changes when you join computers together?

states.label: Stand-alone computer
points: Files only on that computer
Needs its own printer
Software installed one machine at a time
Viruses cannot spread to other machines

states.label: Networked computer
points: Log on anywhere and open your files
Shares printers and the internet connection
Updates installed on every machine at once
Needs security to stop viruses and hackers

blocks.text: When you log on in the computer room, your work is not saved on the computer in front of you. It is saved on a **server** somewhere else in the school, and you can open it from any computer in the building. That only works because the computers are joined together in a **[[Network]]**.

A network is **two or more computers or devices connected together** so that they can communicate and share data and resources. The connection can be a cable or a wireless signal. A computer that is not connected to anything is called a **[[Stand-alone computer]]**.
Why do we network computers?

items: **Share files:** pupils and teachers can save work centrally and open it on any computer.
**Share hardware:** thirty pupils can use one printer instead of needing thirty printers.
**Share an internet connection:** every device uses the same connection to the outside world.
**Communicate:** email, Teams messages and video calls all travel over networks.
**Central management:** the technician can install software or updates on every computer at once, and back up everyone's work in one go.
**Security and logins:** each user has their own username and password, and can only see the files they are allowed to.

blocks.text: Are there any drawbacks?

head: Drawback
Why it matters
rows: Servers, switches, cables and wireless access points all cost money to buy and install.
Large networks need a trained technician or network manager to run them.
Malware on one computer can travel across the network to others.
If the main server goes down, nobody can get to their files.
A network that is connected to the internet can be attacked from outside, so it needs security such as a firewall.
blocks.caption: Disadvantages of networking

blocks.text: LAN or WAN?

head: LAN
WAN
rows: Large: towns, countries, the whole world
The organisation itself, e.g. the school
The school network; your home Wi-Fi
The internet; a bank linking all its branches

blocks.title: Worked example: LAN or WAN?
blocks.context: A supermarket chain has a network in each of its 40 shops. The tills in every shop send sales data to head office in Belfast each night. Which networks are LANs and which is a WAN?
steps: Inside a single shop, the tills, office PCs and printer are all on one site, so each shop has a **LAN**.
The shops are spread across Northern Ireland, so the connections linking all 40 LANs to head office cover a large area.
A network linking LANs across a large area is a **WAN**.
blocks.answer: Each shop is a LAN; the network joining the shops to head office is a WAN.

blocks.text: The **[[Internet]]** is a giant WAN: millions of LANs (homes, schools, businesses) joined together all over the world. When you browse from school, your request leaves the school LAN and travels across the internet.
In Year 8 you met the difference between the internet and the World Wide Web. In this topic we look under the bonnet at **how** networks actually move data around.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A network is two or more connected devices that can share data and resources.
Networks let us share files, printers and an internet connection, and manage computers centrally.
Drawbacks include cost, the spread of viruses and dependence on the server.
LAN = small area (one site); WAN = large area, often linking LANs.
The internet is the largest WAN in the world.

check.q: What is a network?
o: A single computer with lots of storage
Two or more devices connected so they can share data and resources
check.why: A network needs at least two connected devices.

check.q: Which of these is a LAN?
o: A bank linking branches in five countries
check.why: One school site is a small area, so it is a LAN.

check.q: Which is a **disadvantage** of networking computers?
o: Viruses can spread from one computer to others
Work can be backed up centrally
check.why: Being connected means malware can travel between computers.

check.q: What is the largest WAN in the world?
check.why: The internet links millions of networks worldwide.

practice.q: State **three** advantages of connecting the computers in a school to a network.
practice.a: Any three: share files / log on and open work from any computer (1); share printers or other hardware (1); share one internet connection (1); communicate, e.g. email/messages (1); install software or updates centrally (1); back up all users' work centrally (1); individual logins control who can access what (1).

practice.q: Explain the difference between a LAN and a WAN. Give an example of each.
practice.a: LAN covers a small geographical area / one site (1); e.g. a school or home network (1). WAN covers a large geographical area / links LANs together (1); e.g. the internet or a company linking branches (1).

practice.q: Give **two** disadvantages of a network.
practice.a: Any two: cost of hardware/cabling (1); need a technician to manage it (1); viruses can spread across it (1); if the server fails users cannot access files (1); risk of hacking (1).

pages.spec: Identify the main pieces of network hardware and describe what each one does
pages.summary: Every device needs a NIC to join a network. Switches connect devices inside a LAN, routers connect networks together, wireless access points add Wi-Fi, and modems convert signals. Data travels through Ethernet or fibre optic cables.

diagram.title: Match the hardware
diagram.caption: Click to match each device with its job.
pairs: Lets a device connect to a network; has a MAC address built in
Connects devices inside a LAN and sends data only to the right one
Connects different networks, such as a LAN and the internet
Lets laptops and phones join a wired network by Wi-Fi
Converts digital data into signals for a phone line or cable
Carries data as pulses of light over long distances

blocks.text: A network needs more than just computers. Special hardware connects the devices and moves data between them. If you look in the cupboard in the corner of a computer room you will often find a **cabinet** full of flashing lights and cables: that is network hardware at work.
The main devices

head: Hardware
What it does
Where you might see it
rows: Lets a device connect to a network. Every NIC has a unique **MAC address** built in. It can be wired (with an Ethernet socket) or wireless.
Built into every laptop, phone, games console and smart TV
Connects lots of devices together **inside a LAN**. It reads where each piece of data is going and sends it **only to the device it is meant for**.
The network cabinet in school, with dozens of cables plugged in
Connects **different networks together**, for example the school LAN to the internet. It forwards packets towards their destination using **IP addresses**.
Your broadband box at home; the school's link to the outside world
Lets wireless devices join a wired network using Wi-Fi.
White boxes on classroom ceilings or corridor walls
Converts the computer's digital data into signals that can travel along a phone line or cable, and converts incoming signals back. (Short for **mo**dulator **dem**odulator.)
Usually built into a home broadband router
blocks.caption: Network hardware

blocks.text: A quick way to remember: a **switch** works **within** one network; a **router** works **between** networks.
Your home router is several devices in one

The box your internet provider sends you is usually called a router, but it actually contains a **router**, a **switch** (the yellow Ethernet sockets on the back), a **wireless access point** (for Wi-Fi) and often a **modem** (to talk to the phone line or fibre). In a school these are separate, bigger devices because there are hundreds of users.
Cables

head: Ethernet (copper)
Fibre optic
rows: Electrical signals along twisted pairs of copper wire
Pulses of light along thin strands of glass
Can be affected by electrical interference
More expensive and harder to fit
Connecting PCs to the switch in a classroom
Linking buildings on a school site; broadband to homes and streets

blocks.title: Worked example: following the journey out of school
blocks.context: You click a link in a lesson. Which pieces of hardware does your request pass through to get from your PC to the internet?
steps: The **NIC** in your PC turns the request into signals and sends them down the **Ethernet cable**.
The cable runs to a **switch** in the network cabinet, which passes the data on towards the school router.
The **router** sees the data is for a computer outside the school and forwards it onto the internet (often via a **fibre optic** link).
blocks.answer: NIC, Ethernet cable, switch, router, then out onto the internet.

blocks.text: You may also hear of a **hub**. It is an older, simpler device that sends every piece of data to every device connected to it. Switches replaced hubs because they are cleverer and cause less wasted traffic.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A NIC lets a device connect to a network and holds its MAC address.
A switch connects devices within a LAN and sends data only to the right device.
A router connects networks together and forwards data using IP addresses.
A wireless access point adds Wi-Fi to a wired network; a modem converts signals for phone lines or cables.
Ethernet uses copper and electricity; fibre optic uses glass and light, and is faster over longer distances.

check.q: Which device connects a school LAN to the internet?
check.why: Routers connect different networks together.

check.q: What does a switch do?
o: Connects devices within a LAN and sends data to the correct device
Gives each device a MAC address
check.why: A switch works inside one network.

check.q: How does a fibre optic cable carry data?
o: As pulses of light in glass
check.why: Fibre uses light, so it is fast and unaffected by electrical interference.

check.q: Which piece of hardware must every networked device have?
check.why: Without a NIC, a device cannot connect to any network.

practice.q: Describe the purpose of a **router** and a **switch**.
practice.a: Router: connects different networks together / connects the LAN to the internet (1); forwards packets towards their destination using IP addresses (1). Switch: connects devices together within a LAN (1); sends data only to the device it is intended for (1).

practice.q: A school is linking its main building to a new sports hall 400 metres away. Explain why fibre optic cable would be chosen instead of Ethernet cable.
practice.a: Any three: Ethernet only works up to about 100 m (1); fibre works over many kilometres (1); fibre is faster / higher bandwidth (1); fibre is not affected by electrical interference (1).

practice.q: What is the job of a wireless access point?
practice.a: It allows wireless devices to connect to a wired network using Wi-Fi (1).

pages.spec: Compare wired and wireless connections, including Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, and choose a suitable one for a task
pages.summary: Wired connections are faster, more reliable and more secure. Wireless connections (Wi-Fi and Bluetooth) give freedom to move and need no cables, but are slower, have limited range and can suffer from interference.

diagram.title: Which connection?
diagram.caption: Decide, then click to check.
head: Situation
Best connection
Reason
rows: Desktop PCs in the computer room
They never move and need speed and reliability
Smartwatch sending steps to a phone
Close together and needs very little battery power
Pupils using laptops in the library
They move around and need internet access
Linking two school buildings 500 m apart
Too far for Ethernet or Wi-Fi; fibre is fast over long distances
Short range, low power, two devices
Must be as fast, reliable and secure as possible

blocks.text: Devices can connect to a network in two ways: with a **cable** (wired) or using **radio waves** (wireless). Most schools use both. The desktop PCs in the computer room are wired, while laptops, iPads and phones connect wirelessly.
Wired vs wireless

head: Wired (e.g. Ethernet)
Wireless (e.g. Wi-Fi)
rows: Usually slower; drops as you move away or more people join
Harder to intercept: someone needs to plug in
Signals travel through the air, so must be encrypted and password protected
Cables must be run through walls and ceilings
Quick to set up; no trailing cables

blocks.text: Wi-Fi

**[[Wi-Fi]]** uses radio waves to connect devices to a wireless access point or home router. A typical indoor range is **a few tens of metres**, and the signal gets weaker through thick walls and floors. To join a Wi-Fi network you usually need its name and a password (the **key**), which also **encrypts** the data so people nearby cannot read it.
Bluetooth

**[[Bluetooth]]** is also wireless, but it is designed for **short-range** connections (usually up to about **10 metres**) directly between two devices. It uses very little power, which makes it perfect for small battery-powered gadgets. Devices are **paired** once and then reconnect automatically.

head: Wi-Fi
Bluetooth
rows: Fast enough to stream films and games
Laptops and phones on the school or home network; internet access
Wireless earbuds, game controllers, smartwatches, sending a photo to a friend's phone
blocks.caption: Wi-Fi compared with Bluetooth

blocks.title: Worked example: choosing a connection
blocks.context: The school is setting up three things: (a) a new server in the network cabinet, (b) iPads for a geography field trip around the school grounds, (c) a wireless speaker for the PE department's phone. Which connection suits each?
steps: (a) A server must be fast and reliable and it never moves, so use a **wired Ethernet** (or fibre) connection.
(b) Pupils will walk around, so the iPads need **Wi-Fi**, with access points covering the grounds.
(c) A phone and a speaker a few metres apart only need a short-range, low-power link, so use **Bluetooth**.
blocks.answer: Server: wired. iPads: Wi-Fi. Speaker: Bluetooth.

blocks.text: Free public Wi-Fi in cafés is often **not encrypted**. Avoid logging in to anything important, such as a bank account, on it.
If your games console keeps lagging online, try plugging it straight into the router with an Ethernet cable. A wired link is usually faster and steadier than Wi-Fi.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Wired connections are faster, more reliable and more secure, but you cannot move around.
Wireless connections give freedom to move and need no cables, but are slower and can suffer interference.
Wi-Fi connects devices to a network over tens of metres.
Bluetooth connects two devices directly over about 10 metres using very little power.
Wireless data should be encrypted with a password so others cannot read it.

check.q: Which is an advantage of a wired connection over Wi-Fi?
o: You can walk around with your device
It is usually faster and more reliable
check.why: Cables give a steady, fast connection.

check.q: What is the typical range of Bluetooth?
check.why: Bluetooth is designed for short-range links.

check.q: Which would be the best use of Bluetooth?
o: Connecting wireless earbuds to a phone
check.why: Short range, low power, two devices: ideal for Bluetooth.

check.q: Why should a Wi-Fi network have a password?
o: To stop strangers joining and to encrypt the data
check.why: The key controls who can join and scrambles the data.

practice.q: Give **two** advantages and **two** disadvantages of using Wi-Fi rather than cables in a classroom.
practice.a: Advantages, any two: pupils can move around / use laptops anywhere (1); no trailing cables / safer (1); cheaper and quicker to install (1); easy to add new devices (1). Disadvantages, any two: slower (1); less reliable / interference from walls or other devices (1); limited range (1); less secure / signals can be intercepted (1).

practice.q: Describe **two** differences between Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.
practice.a: Any two: Bluetooth has a shorter range (about 10 m) than Wi-Fi (tens of metres) (1); Bluetooth uses less power (1); Bluetooth is slower (1); Bluetooth connects two devices directly while Wi-Fi connects devices to a network/the internet (1).

pages.spec: Describe star, bus and mesh network topologies and give an advantage and a disadvantage of each
pages.summary: A topology is the layout of a network. In a star, every device connects to a central switch. In a bus, every device shares one backbone cable. In a mesh, devices connect to many others so there are lots of routes.

diagram.title: Star, bus and mesh
diagram.caption: Click each layout to compare them.

states.label: Star
points: Every device cabled to a central switch
One broken cable affects only one device
Switch fails = whole network fails
Used in most schools and offices

states.label: Bus
points: All devices on one backbone cable
Cheap: needs little cable
Backbone breaks = whole network fails
Data can collide when two devices send at once

states.label: Mesh
points: Devices connected to several others
Many routes, so very reliable
Lots of cable: expensive to set up
The internet and mesh Wi-Fi work this way

blocks.text: A **[[Topology]]** is the **shape or layout** of a network: how the devices are connected to each other. Different layouts suit different jobs, and each has strengths and weaknesses.
Star topology
In a **[[Star topology]]**, every computer has **its own cable to a central switch**. This is how most school and office networks are built, including the computer rooms in our school.

items: **Advantage:** if one cable breaks, only that one computer loses its connection; everyone else carries on.
**Advantage:** it is fast, because the switch sends data only to the computer it is meant for.
**Advantage:** it is easy to add a new computer: just plug another cable into the switch.
**Disadvantage:** if the central switch fails, the whole network goes down.
**Disadvantage:** it needs a lot of cable, because every device has its own.

blocks.text: Bus topology

In a **[[Bus topology]]**, every device is connected to **one main cable**, called the **backbone**, with a **terminator** at each end to stop signals bouncing back. Data sent by one device travels along the whole backbone, and each device checks whether it is meant for them. Bus networks are rarely used today, but they help explain why star networks took over.

items: **Advantage:** cheap and simple, because it needs less cable.
**Disadvantage:** if the backbone cable breaks, the **whole network fails**.
**Disadvantage:** only one device can send at a time. If two send at once their data **collides**, so it gets slower as more devices are added.
**Disadvantage:** every device can see all the data, which is less secure.

blocks.text: Mesh topology

In a **[[Mesh topology]]**, devices are connected to **several other devices**. In a **full mesh** every device connects to every other one; in a **partial mesh** some do. Because there are lots of routes, if one link breaks the data simply takes another path. **The internet is a giant partial mesh** of routers. Many homes now use **mesh Wi-Fi**, where several small units around the house pass data between each other to cover every room.

items: **Advantage:** very reliable: there is no single point of failure.
**Advantage:** data can take the quickest or least busy route.
**Disadvantage:** a wired mesh needs huge amounts of cable and is expensive to set up and manage.

blocks.title: Worked example: how much cable does a full mesh need?
blocks.context: A full mesh network has 5 computers, each connected directly to every other one. How many cables are needed? How many would a star network with 5 computers need?
steps: Each computer connects to the other 4, so 5 x 4 = 20 connection ends.
Each cable has two ends (it joins two computers), so divide by 2: 20 / 2 = **10 cables**.
A star needs one cable from each computer to the switch: **5 cables**.
Check: with 6 computers a full mesh needs 6 x 5 / 2 = 15 cables, while a star needs 6. The mesh grows much faster.
blocks.answer: Full mesh: 10 cables. Star: 5 cables. This is why wired full meshes are rare in schools.

blocks.text: Exam questions often ask: *what happens if one cable fails?* Star: only that device is affected. Bus: the whole network if it is the backbone. Mesh: data takes another route.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Topology = the layout of a network.
Star: each device connects to a central switch; one cable failing only affects one device, but the switch is a single point of failure.
Bus: all devices share one backbone; cheap, but a break stops everything and data can collide.
Mesh: many connections and routes; very reliable but expensive. The internet is a mesh.
Most school networks use a star topology.

check.q: In a star topology, what is at the centre?
check.why: Every device has its own cable to the central switch.

check.q: What happens in a bus network if the backbone cable breaks?
check.why: Every device relies on the single backbone.

check.q: Why is a mesh network very reliable?
o: There are many routes, so data can go around a broken link
check.why: No single point of failure.

check.q: Which topology is most like the internet?
check.why: The internet is a huge partial mesh of routers.

practice.q: Describe a star topology and give **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of it.
practice.a: Each device has its own cable to a central switch (1). Advantage, any one: if one cable fails only that device is affected / fast / easy to add devices (1). Disadvantage, any one: if the switch fails the whole network fails / uses a lot of cable, so more expensive (1).

practice.q: Explain why a mesh topology is more reliable than a bus topology.
practice.a: In a mesh, devices have several connections / there are many routes, so if one link fails data takes another route (1). In a bus, all devices rely on one backbone cable, so if it breaks the whole network fails (1).

practice.q: A full mesh network has 4 computers. How many cables are needed? Show your working.
practice.a: 4 x 3 = 12 connection ends, divided by 2 (1) = 6 cables (1).

pages.spec: Compare client-server and peer-to-peer networks and decide which is suitable for a given situation
pages.summary: In a client-server network, clients ask central servers for files, logins and services, so it is easy to manage and secure. In a peer-to-peer network every computer is equal and shares directly, which is cheap and simple but harder to manage.

diagram.title: Client-server or peer-to-peer?
diagram.caption: Decide, then click to check.
head: Situation
Best model
Reason
rows: A school with 900 pupils who log on anywhere
Two friends swapping photos with AirDrop
A family sharing a printer between two laptops
A bank with thousands of staff
Watching a video on a website
Your browser is a client asking a web server
A small shop with one till and one office PC
Cheap and simple for two computers

blocks.text: As well as a physical layout, every network has a way of **organising who does what**. There are two main models: **client-server** and **peer-to-peer**.
Client-server

In a **[[Client-server network]]**, one or more powerful computers called **[[servers|Server]]** provide services, and the other computers, called **[[clients|Client]]**, request them. The school network (C2k) is client-server: when you log on, your PC (the client) asks a server to check your username and password, and then loads your files from a file server.

head: Type of server
What it does
School example
rows: Stores users' files and controls who can open them
Your documents and the shared Year 9 folder
Manages a queue of print jobs for shared printers
Choosing a printer in the computer room
Stores web pages and sends them to browsers that ask for them
Checks usernames and passwords when people log on
Logging on at the start of the lesson
blocks.caption: Common types of server

blocks.text: Peer-to-peer

In a **[[Peer-to-peer network]]** (P2P) there is **no central server**. Every computer, called a **peer**, is equal. Each one stores its own files and can share them directly with the others. Sending a photo to a friend's phone with Bluetooth or AirDrop, or connecting two laptops to swap a file, are simple examples. Some online games and file-sharing apps also use P2P.

head: Client-server
Peer-to-peer
rows: Each user must back up their own computer
Central logins and permissions; easier to control
Harder to control; each user sets their own sharing
Clients are fine unless it is the server
Only that computer's files are lost to others
Homes, very small offices, sharing between friends

blocks.title: Worked example: which model?
blocks.context: A hairdresser has two computers: one at the reception desk for bookings and one in the back office for accounts. A grammar school has 600 computers and 1,000 users. Which model suits each?
steps: The hairdresser only has two computers and probably no IT technician. Buying a server would be expensive and unnecessary, so **peer-to-peer** is suitable: the two computers can share files and a printer directly.
The school has hundreds of users who need to log on anywhere, have their work backed up and be kept out of each other's files. This needs central control, so **client-server** is suitable.

blocks.text: When you visit a website, your browser is acting as a **client** and the computer storing the website is a **web server**. So the internet itself relies on the client-server model millions of times every second.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Client-server: clients request services from central servers.
Servers can store files, manage printing, host websites, handle email and check logins.
Peer-to-peer: no server; every computer is equal and shares directly.
Client-server is easier to secure, back up and manage, but costs more.
Peer-to-peer is cheap and simple, so suits homes and very small businesses.

check.q: What is a client?
o: A computer that provides services to others
A computer that requests services from a server
check.why: Clients ask; servers provide.

check.q: Which network model has no central server?
check.why: In P2P every computer is equal.

check.q: Why does a school use a client-server network?
o: Logins, security and backups can be managed centrally
check.why: Central control suits hundreds of users.

check.q: Which server checks your username and password when you log on?
check.why: Authentication means checking who you are.

practice.q: Describe **two** differences between a client-server network and a peer-to-peer network.
practice.a: Any two differences, each explained for both sides (2 marks each, max 4): client-server has a central server, P2P has none / all computers equal (2); client-server stores files centrally, P2P stores files on each computer (2); client-server is backed up centrally, P2P each user backs up their own (2); client-server security controlled centrally, P2P harder to control (2); client-server more expensive, P2P cheaper (2).

practice.q: State **three** types of server and what each does.
practice.a: Any three, 1 mark each for type with correct job: file server, stores users' files (1); print server, manages print jobs/queue (1); web server, stores and sends web pages (1); email server, sends/receives/stores email (1); authentication server, checks usernames and passwords (1).

pages.spec: Explain how data is split into packets and sent across a network using packet switching
pages.summary: Data is split into small packets. Each packet has a header with the sender's and receiver's addresses and a packet number. Routers send each packet by the best route available, and the receiving computer puts them back in order and asks for any missing ones again.

diagram.title: A packet's journey
diagram.caption: Click each step to follow a file across the internet.

nodes.label: Split
nodes.detail: The sender's computer splits the file into numbered packets and adds a header to each.

nodes.label: Send
nodes.detail: Packets leave through the router onto the internet.

nodes.label: Route
nodes.detail: Each router reads the destination address and sends each packet by the best route at that moment.

nodes.label: Reorder
nodes.detail: Packets arrive, possibly out of order; they are sorted using their packet numbers.

nodes.label: Check and rebuild
nodes.detail: Any missing or damaged packet is requested again, then the file is put back together.

blocks.text: When you send a photo to a friend, it is not sent as one big lump. It is chopped into lots of small pieces called **[[packets|Packet]]**. Each packet travels across the internet on its own, and the pieces are put back together at the other end.
What is in a packet?

head: Part
What it contains
Like on a parcel...
rows: The sender's IP address, the destination IP address, the packet number (e.g. 3 of 50) and the protocol being used
The address label and return address
The actual piece of data: part of your photo, message or web page
A check value used to spot if the data was damaged on the way, and a marker for the end of the packet
A seal showing it has not been tampered with
blocks.caption: The parts of a packet

blocks.text: Packet switching

The internet uses **[[Packet switching]]**. Each packet is sent separately. At every **router** it reaches, the router reads the destination address in the header and sends the packet onwards along whichever route is **best at that moment**. If one route is busy or broken, the next packet can be sent a different way. This means packets from the same file can travel by **different routes** and arrive **out of order**.

blocks.title: Worked example: sending a photo from Enniskillen to Australia
blocks.context: Orla emails a 2 MB photo to her cousin in Sydney. To keep it simple, imagine it is split into just 6 packets. Packet 4 goes missing on the way. What happens?
steps: Orla's computer splits the photo into packets 1 to 6 and adds a **header** to each one with her IP address, her cousin's mail server's IP address and the packet number.
The packets leave through her router. Routers along the way send each packet by the best route at that moment: packets 1, 2 and 5 go via London and New York; 3 and 6 go via Amsterdam and Singapore.
They arrive in the order 1, 3, 2, 6, 5. The receiving computer uses the **packet numbers** to put them back in order: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6.
It notices packet 4 is missing, so it asks for packet 4 to be **sent again**.
Packet 4 arrives, the photo is reassembled perfectly, and an acknowledgement is sent back.
blocks.answer: The packets travel separately, are reordered using their numbers, and any missing packet is resent, so the photo arrives complete.

blocks.text: Why use packets?

items: **Reliable:** if a route breaks, packets simply go another way, and lost packets can be resent.
**Efficient:** many people share the same cables at once, because packets from different users take turns.
**Only damaged parts are resent:** if one packet is damaged, only that small packet is sent again, not the whole file.
**Fast:** packets can avoid busy routes.

blocks.text: Protocols

For this to work, every device in the world must follow the same rules. A set of rules for communicating is called a **[[Protocol]]**. **TCP/IP** is the main set of protocols for the internet: **TCP** splits data into packets, numbers them and checks they all arrive; **IP** handles the addressing and routing. **HTTP** and **HTTPS** are the protocols for sending web pages.
Think of a jigsaw sent through the post in several envelopes. Each envelope is numbered, they may arrive on different days, but you can still build the picture using the numbers.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Data is split into small packets before it is sent.
Each packet has a header (sender and destination addresses, packet number), a payload and a trailer.
Routers send each packet by the best available route, so packets may arrive out of order.
The receiver reorders packets using their numbers and asks for missing ones to be resent.
A protocol is a set of rules for communication; TCP/IP is the main one for the internet.

check.q: Which part of a packet contains the destination address?
check.why: The header is like the address label on a parcel.

check.q: Why might packets arrive in the wrong order?
o: They are sent by different routes
check.why: Each packet may take a different route, some quicker than others.

check.q: What happens if a packet goes missing?
o: The receiver asks for that packet to be sent again
The other packets are thrown away
check.why: Only the missing packet needs resending.

check.q: What is a protocol?
o: A set of rules for how devices communicate
check.why: Everyone follows the same rules, so devices can understand each other.

practice.q: State **three** items of information found in the header of a packet.
practice.a: Any three: sender's/source IP address (1); destination IP address (1); packet number / sequence number (1); total number of packets (1); protocol used (1).

practice.q: Describe how a file is sent across the internet using packet switching.
practice.a: Any four: the file is split into packets (1); each packet is given a header with addresses and a packet number (1); routers send each packet by the best route available / packets can take different routes (1); packets may arrive out of order (1); the receiver reassembles them in order using the packet numbers (1); missing or damaged packets are requested again (1).

pages.spec: Explain what IP addresses and MAC addresses are and the difference between them
pages.summary: An IP address identifies a device on a network so data can be routed to it, and it can change. A MAC address is a unique, permanent address built into a device's NIC when it is made.

diagram.title: IP or MAC?
diagram.caption: Click to match each address fact with its description.
pairs: A much longer address created because IPv4 ran out
12 hexadecimal digits fixed in the NIC by the manufacturer
Uses IP addresses to send packets between networks
Uses MAC addresses to send data within a LAN

blocks.text: For a packet to reach the right device, every device needs an **address**, just as every house needs an address for the post to arrive. Networked devices actually have **two** kinds: an **IP address** and a **MAC address**.
IP addresses
An **[[IP address]]** (Internet Protocol address) identifies a device on a network so that data can be **routed** to it. Routers use IP addresses to decide where to send packets.

items: **IPv4** addresses are four numbers, each from **0 to 255**, separated by dots, e.g. `192.168.1.25`. That gives about 4.3 billion different addresses.

There are now far more devices than that, so **IPv6** was created. IPv6 addresses are much longer and written in hexadecimal, e.g. `2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334`. There are enough for every grain of sand on Earth to have many.
IP addresses are usually given out automatically by the router when a device joins a network, so **they can change**. Your phone gets a different IP address at home, at school and in a café.

blocks.title: Worked example: is this a valid IPv4 address?
blocks.context: Which of these are valid IPv4 addresses? (a) 10.0.15.200 (b) 192.168.1.256 (c) 172.16.4 (d) 8.8.8.8
steps: Rule: exactly **four** numbers separated by dots, each from **0 to 255**.
(a) 10, 0, 15, 200: four numbers, all 0 to 255, so **valid**.
(b) 256 is bigger than 255, so **not valid**.
(c) Only three numbers, so **not valid**.
(d) 8, 8, 8, 8: four numbers, all in range, so **valid**.
blocks.answer: (a) and (d) are valid; (b) and (c) are not.

blocks.text: MAC addresses

A **[[MAC address]]** (Media Access Control address) is **built into the NIC** of a device when it is manufactured. It is **unique** in the world and **does not normally change**. It is written as **12 hexadecimal digits** in pairs, e.g. `3C:22:FB:9A:41:07`. Switches use MAC addresses to send data to the right device **within a LAN**.
IP vs MAC

head: IP address
MAC address
rows: A device's location on a network
The NIC of one particular device
Yes: it changes when you join a different network
No: fixed when the NIC is made
Routers, to send data between networks
Switches, to send data within a LAN

blocks.text: Think of a MAC address as your **name**: it stays with you wherever you go. An IP address is like your **postal address**: if you move house, it changes.

Devices on a home or school LAN usually have **private** IP addresses (often starting 192.168 or 10). The router has one **public** IP address that the rest of the internet sees, and it keeps track of which device inside asked for what.

blocks.title: Key points
items: An IP address identifies a device on a network so data can be routed to it.
IPv4 = four numbers 0 to 255 separated by dots; IPv6 is longer and has far more addresses.
IP addresses are usually assigned by the router and can change.
A MAC address is unique, set in the NIC when it is made, and does not change.
Routers use IP addresses; switches use MAC addresses.

check.q: Which is a valid IPv4 address?
check.why: Four numbers, each 0 to 255.

check.q: Where is a MAC address stored?
o: In the NIC, when it is made
check.why: The manufacturer builds it into the network interface card.

check.q: Why was IPv6 introduced?
o: The world was running out of IPv4 addresses
check.why: IPv4 only has about 4.3 billion addresses.

check.q: Your phone connects to Wi-Fi at school, then at home. What happens?
o: Its IP address will probably change but its MAC address stays the same
check.why: IP addresses depend on the network; MAC addresses are fixed.

practice.q: Describe **two** differences between an IP address and a MAC address.
practice.a: Any two differences, each explained for both sides (2 marks each, max 4): IP can change / MAC is permanent (2); IP is assigned by the router/network / MAC is set by the manufacturer (2); IP is used to route data between networks / MAC is used to identify a device within a LAN (2); IPv4 is four denary numbers / MAC is 12 hexadecimal digits (2).

practice.q: Explain why 192.168.0.260 is not a valid IPv4 address.
practice.a: Each number in an IPv4 address must be between 0 and 255, and 260 is greater than 255 (1).

pages.spec: Describe, step by step, what happens when you type a URL into a browser, including the role of DNS
pages.summary: Computers find each other using IP addresses, but people remember names. When you type a URL, a DNS server looks up the IP address for the domain name, then the browser contacts the web server at that address and the page arrives as packets.

diagram.title: Typing a URL: step by step
diagram.caption: Click each step to see what happens.

nodes.label: Type the URL
nodes.detail: You type www.bbc.co.uk and press Enter.

nodes.label: IP address in cache?
nodes.detail: The browser checks whether it already knows the IP address from a recent visit.

nodes.label: Ask a DNS server
nodes.detail: If not, a DNS server (usually your ISP's) looks it up, asking other DNS servers if needed.

nodes.label: IP address returned
nodes.detail: The matching IP address is sent back and cached for next time.

nodes.label: Request the page
nodes.detail: The browser asks the web server at that IP address for the page.

nodes.label: Page arrives and displays
nodes.detail: The page comes back as packets, which the browser reassembles and shows.

blocks.text: Every website lives on a **[[Web server]]** with an IP address. But nobody wants to type a number like `151.101.0.81` to read the news. We use **[[domain names|Domain name]]** like `bbc.co.uk` instead. Something has to translate the name into the number, and that something is **[[DNS]]**.
Parts of a URL

head: Part
Example
Meaning
rows: The rules for sending the page; the **s** means it is secure (encrypted)
Part of the website, often www for World Wide Web
The name of the website, which DNS turns into an IP address
The particular page or folder on the web server
blocks.caption: Breaking down https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football

blocks.text: The whole address is called a **[[URL]]** (Uniform Resource Locator).
DNS: the internet's phone book

The **Domain Name System** is a huge network of **DNS servers** around the world. Together they hold a directory that matches domain names to IP addresses, just as your phone's contacts match names to phone numbers. No single server knows everything, so they ask each other.
What happens when you type a URL

blocks.title: Worked example: visiting www.bbc.co.uk/sport
blocks.context: You type https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport into Chrome and press Enter. What happens before the page appears?
steps: The browser checks its own **cache** (memory) to see if it already knows the IP address from a recent visit. If it does, it skips to step 5.
If not, your computer sends a request to a **DNS server**, usually one run by your **[[ISP]]** (or the school's network): *What is the IP address of www.bbc.co.uk?*
If that DNS server does not know, it asks other DNS servers, working from the top: one that knows about **.uk**, then one that knows about **bbc.co.uk**.
The IP address is found and sent back to your computer. It is also remembered (cached) to make the next visit quicker.
Your browser sends a request to the **web server** at that IP address: *Please send me the page /sport*.
The web server sends the page back, split into **packets**.
Your browser reassembles the packets and displays the page. Images and videos on the page may each need further requests.
blocks.answer: DNS turns the domain name into an IP address; the browser then requests the page from the web server at that address, and it arrives in packets.

blocks.text: If a DNS server is not working, websites will not load by name even though your internet connection is fine. It can look as though *the internet is down* when only DNS is broken.
All of this usually happens in **less than a second**. Caching is the reason a website you visit often loads faster than a brand-new one.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Computers use IP addresses; people use domain names.
A URL is made of a protocol, domain name and path.
DNS servers translate domain names into IP addresses, like a phone book.
Steps: check cache, ask DNS server, get IP address, request page from web server, page arrives in packets, browser displays it.
If DNS fails, sites cannot be found by name.

check.q: What does DNS do?
o: Stores all the web pages in the world
Translates domain names into IP addresses
check.why: It is the internet's phone book.

check.q: In https://www.ergs.org/sport, which part is the path?
check.why: The path picks the page on the web server.

check.q: What does the browser do **after** it receives the IP address?
o: Sends a request for the page to the web server at that IP address
check.why: Now it knows where the website lives, it can ask for the page.

check.q: Why does a website you visit often load faster?
o: The IP address is cached, so DNS lookup can be skipped
check.why: Caching saves the lookup step.

practice.q: Explain why the Domain Name System (DNS) is needed.
practice.a: Computers find each other using IP addresses (1), but people find domain names easier to remember than numbers, so DNS translates the name into the IP address (1).

practice.q: Describe the steps that take place when a user types a URL into a web browser until the page is displayed.
practice.a: Any five, in a sensible order: browser checks its cache for the IP address (1); request sent to a DNS server (1); DNS server looks up the domain name / asks other DNS servers if it does not know (1); IP address returned to the computer (1); browser sends a request to the web server at that IP address (1); web server sends the page back in packets (1); browser reassembles and displays the page (1).

practice.q: Name the **three** main parts of the URL https://www.example.co.uk/news.
practice.a: Protocol: https (1); domain name: www.example.co.uk or example.co.uk (1); path: /news (1).

pages.spec: Explain bandwidth and network speed units, and calculate how long a file will take to download
pages.summary: Bandwidth is how much data a connection can carry each second, measured in bits per second (usually Mbps). To find a download time, convert the file size into megabits (multiply MB by 8) and divide by the speed in Mbps.

diagram.title: How long will it take to download?
diagram.caption: Change the file size (MB) and the connection speed (Mbps) to see the download time.

blocks.text: Broadband adverts boast about speeds like *up to 500 Mb*. But what does that actually mean, and how long will that new game take to download?
Bandwidth

**[[Bandwidth]]** is the **maximum amount of data that can be sent each second** across a connection. Think of it like the number of lanes on a motorway: more lanes means more cars (data) can travel at once. If lots of people share the same connection, such as a whole family streaming at the same time, each gets a smaller share.
Speed units: bits, not bytes
Network speed, or **bit rate**, is measured in **bits per second**, not bytes. Watch the letter **b**: a small **b** means **bits**, a capital **B** means **bytes**. There are **8 bits in a byte**.

head: Unit
Stands for
Bits per second
blocks.caption: Network speed units go up in thousands

blocks.text: File sizes are usually in **megabytes (MB)** but speeds are in **megabits per second (Mbps)**. You must **multiply the file size by 8** to turn megabytes into megabits before dividing by the speed.
Calculating download time
Download time (seconds) = **file size in megabits / speed in Mbps**. So the method is:

items: Make sure the file size is in **MB** (to keep things simple in speed questions, use 1 GB = 1000 MB).
Multiply by **8** to get **megabits** (Mb).
Divide by the speed in **Mbps** to get the time in **seconds**.
If needed, divide by **60** to turn seconds into minutes.

blocks.title: Worked example 1: downloading a film
blocks.context: A film is 400 MB. Your broadband speed is 50 Mbps. How long will it take to download?
steps: Convert to megabits: 400 MB x 8 = **3,200 Mb**.
Divide by the speed: 3,200 / 50 = **64 seconds**.
In minutes: 64 seconds = **1 minute 4 seconds**.
Check: 50 Mbps x 64 s = 3,200 Mb, and 3,200 / 8 = 400 MB. Correct.

blocks.title: Worked example 2: downloading a game
blocks.context: A game update is 2 GB. The school connection gives you 100 Mbps. How long will it take?
steps: Convert to MB: 2 GB = 2 x 1000 = **2,000 MB**.
Convert to megabits: 2,000 x 8 = **16,000 Mb**.
Divide by the speed: 16,000 / 100 = **160 seconds**.
In minutes: 160 / 60 = 2 remainder 40, so **2 minutes 40 seconds**.
Check: 100 Mbps x 160 s = 16,000 Mb, and 16,000 / 8 = 2,000 MB = 2 GB. Correct.

blocks.text: Real downloads usually take a bit longer than the calculation says. The connection may be shared with others, the server sending the file may be busy, and every packet carries extra header information as well as your data.
Speed is not just bandwidth

**[[Latency]]** (often called **ping** or **lag**) is the **delay** before data starts to arrive, measured in milliseconds (ms). For downloading a film, bandwidth matters most. For online gaming or video calls, **low latency** matters more, because you need each action to reach the server instantly.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Bandwidth = the maximum amount of data a connection can carry per second.
Speeds are measured in bits per second: bps, Kbps, Mbps, Gbps (each 1,000 times bigger).
Small b = bits, capital B = bytes; 1 byte = 8 bits.
Download time (s) = file size in MB x 8 / speed in Mbps.
Latency is the delay before data arrives; low latency matters for gaming.

check.q: What does Mbps stand for?
check.why: Small b = bits.

check.q: A 100 MB file is downloaded at 20 Mbps. How long does it take?
Why do you multiply a file size in MB by 8?
check.why: There are 8 bits in every byte.

check.q: Which matters most for a fast-paced online game?
check.why: Low latency means actions reach the server with little delay.

practice.q: Define the term **bandwidth**.
practice.a: The maximum amount of data that can be transmitted across a network/connection per second (1).

practice.q: A pupil wants to download a 600 MB video. Their connection speed is 40 Mbps. Calculate how long the download will take. Show your working.
Give **two** reasons why a download might take longer than the calculated time.
practice.a: Any two: connection shared with other users/devices (1); server sending the file is busy or slow (1); packets carry extra header data (1); Wi-Fi signal weak or interference (1); lost packets have to be resent (1).

pages.spec: Explain what the cloud and the Internet of Things are, and evaluate their benefits and risks
pages.summary: The cloud means using storage and software on servers in data centres over the internet, such as OneDrive. The Internet of Things is everyday objects with sensors that connect to the internet, such as smart speakers and fitness trackers. Both are convenient but raise security and privacy concerns.

diagram.title: A smart home
diagram.caption: Click each device to see how it uses the Internet of Things, and the risk to watch for.

rows.label: Smart speaker
rows.detail: Sends your voice to the cloud to answer questions. Risk: it is always listening for its wake word.

rows.label: Video doorbell
rows.detail: Streams video to your phone. Risk: weak passwords let strangers watch.

rows.label: Smart thermostat
rows.detail: Turn the heating on from the bus home. Risk: shows when nobody is in.

rows.label: Router
rows.detail: Connects every smart device to the internet. Keep its admin password strong.

rows.label: Smart lights
rows.detail: Switch on by voice or timer to save energy. Risk: stop working if the app's servers go down.

rows.label: Fitness tracker
rows.detail: Syncs steps and heart rate to the cloud. Risk: location and health data shared with the company.

rows.label: Smart TV
rows.detail: Streams from cloud services. Risk: may collect data on what you watch.

blocks.text: What is the cloud?

**[[The cloud]]** is not really in the sky. It means using storage, software and services that run on **servers in [[data centres|Data centre]]** owned by big companies, which you reach **over the internet**. When you open a file in OneDrive, write in Google Docs, stream on Netflix or play a game saved online, you are using the cloud.
Cloud storage

**[[Cloud storage]]** means saving your files on someone else's servers rather than on your own device. Examples include **OneDrive**, **Google Drive**, **iCloud** and **Dropbox**. Your school Microsoft 365 account gives you OneDrive, so you can start homework in school and finish it at home.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Open files from any device, anywhere with internet
No internet = no access to your files
Files are safe even if your laptop is lost or broken
You rely on the company not to lose or delete them
Easy to share and work on the same file with others
Shared links can be sent on to the wrong people
Free or cheap; no need to buy extra hard drives
Large amounts of storage need a monthly subscription
Big companies have strong security and encryption
Accounts can be hacked if the password is weak; data may be stored in another country

blocks.text: Turn on **two-factor authentication** for your cloud accounts. Even if someone guesses your password, they still need the code from your phone.
The Internet of Things

The **[[Internet of Things]]** (IoT) is the huge number of **everyday objects** that now contain **sensors** and a **network connection**, so they can collect data and share it over the internet. These are often called **[[smart devices|Smart device]]**. Experts estimate there are now **more IoT devices than people** on Earth.

head: Smart device
What it does
rows: Listens for a wake word, sends your question to the cloud and plays the answer
Counts steps and heart rate and syncs them to an app
Lets you turn the heating on from your phone on the way home
Sends a live video to your phone when someone rings
Turn on and off on a timer or by voice
Measure soil moisture for Fermanagh farmers or show free parking spaces
blocks.caption: Examples of the Internet of Things

blocks.text: Benefits and risks of IoT

head: Benefits
Risks
rows: Stops working if the internet or the company's servers go down
Heating and lights only on when needed
Many devices left on standby still use power
Trackers can alert you to health problems; doorbells deter burglars
Devices with **default passwords** can be hacked and used to spy or attack others
Useful data helps you make decisions
Devices collect lots of personal data: who is home, what you say, where you go

blocks.title: Worked example: securing a new smart camera
blocks.context: Your family buys a wireless smart camera for the front of the house. Give three things you should do to keep it secure.
steps: **Change the default password** straight away to a strong, unique one, because default passwords are published online.
**Install updates** when they appear, because they fix security weaknesses.
**Check the privacy settings** so that video is not shared publicly, and turn on two-factor authentication for the app.
blocks.answer: Change the default password, keep it updated, and check privacy and sharing settings.

blocks.title: Key points
items: The cloud = storage and services on remote servers in data centres, used over the internet.
Cloud storage lets you access, back up and share files anywhere, but needs internet and a trustworthy provider.
The Internet of Things = everyday objects with sensors and internet connections.
IoT brings convenience and energy saving but risks hacking and loss of privacy.
Always change default passwords and keep smart devices updated.

check.q: Which of these is an example of cloud storage?
o: The hard drive in your PC
check.why: OneDrive stores your files on Microsoft's servers.

check.q: What is the main disadvantage of cloud storage?
o: You need an internet connection to access your files
check.why: No connection, no files.

check.q: Which is part of the Internet of Things?
o: A smart thermostat controlled from your phone
check.why: It has sensors and an internet connection.

check.q: Why is it risky to leave a smart device on its default password?
o: Default passwords are widely known, so hackers can get in
check.why: Change it to a strong, unique password.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by **cloud storage** and give **one** example.
practice.a: Files are stored on remote servers / in data centres owned by a company and accessed over the internet (1); example: OneDrive, Google Drive, iCloud, Dropbox (1).

practice.q: Give **two** advantages and **two** disadvantages of a pupil storing their homework in the cloud.
practice.a: Advantages, any two: access from any device/anywhere (1); backed up if laptop lost or broken (1); easy to share/collaborate with others (1); no need to carry a memory stick (1). Disadvantages, any two: needs an internet connection (1); account could be hacked (1); relies on the provider / service could go down (1); may have to pay for more space (1).

practice.q: Describe what the Internet of Things is and give **two** examples.
practice.a: Everyday objects with sensors/network connections that collect and share data over the internet (1). Any two examples: smart speaker, fitness tracker, smart thermostat, video doorbell, smart lights, smart fridge (1 each, max 2).

glossary.def: Two or more computers or devices connected together so they can communicate and share data and resources.
A computer that is not connected to any network.
Local Area Network: a network covering a small area, such as one school, home or office building.
Wide Area Network: a network covering a large geographical area, often linking LANs together. The internet is the largest WAN.
A global WAN made of millions of smaller networks joined together.
Network Interface Card: the hardware inside a device that lets it connect to a network, by cable or wirelessly.
A device that connects devices together within a LAN and sends data only to the device it is meant for.
A device that connects different networks together (e.g. a LAN to the internet) and forwards packets towards their destination.
A device that lets wireless devices connect to a wired network using Wi-Fi.
A device that converts digital data from a computer into signals that can travel along a phone line or cable, and back again.
A copper cable with twisted pairs of wires, used to connect devices in a wired LAN.
A cable that carries data as pulses of light along thin strands of glass; very fast and works over long distances.
A wireless technology that uses radio waves to connect devices to a LAN and the internet, usually over tens of metres.
A short-range, low-power wireless technology for connecting devices directly to each other, usually within about 10 metres.
The layout of a network: how the devices are connected to each other.
A network layout where every device has its own connection to a central switch.
A network layout where all devices are connected to one main cable called the backbone.
A network layout where devices are connected to several other devices, so data has many possible routes.
A powerful computer that provides a service (such as storing files, printing or hosting websites) to other computers on a network.
A computer or device that requests and uses services from a server.
A network where clients request services from one or more central servers, which manage files, logins and security.
A network with no central server, where every computer is equal and shares its own files and resources directly with the others.
A small chunk of data sent across a network, with a header containing information such as the sender's and receiver's addresses and the packet number.
A way of sending data where it is split into packets that may take different routes and are put back in order when they arrive.
A set of rules that devices follow so they can communicate with each other, e.g. TCP/IP or HTTP.
A number that identifies a device on a network so data can be sent to it, e.g. 192.168.1.25. It can change if the device moves to another network.
A unique, permanent address built into every NIC when it is made, written as 12 hexadecimal digits, e.g. 3C:22:FB:9A:41:07.
The human-friendly name of a website, such as bbc.co.uk, that is easier to remember than an IP address.
Domain Name System: a system of servers that translates domain names such as bbc.co.uk into IP addresses.
Internet Service Provider: a company that connects homes and businesses to the internet, e.g. BT or Virgin Media.
Uniform Resource Locator: the full web address of a page, e.g. https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport.
A server that stores web pages and sends them to browsers that request them.
The maximum amount of data that can be sent across a network connection each second.
Megabits per second: one million bits per second. The usual unit for broadband speeds.
The delay between data being sent and it arriving, measured in milliseconds; also called lag or ping.
Services, software and storage provided over the internet from servers in data centres, instead of on your own device.
Saving files on servers owned by a company and accessed over the internet, e.g. OneDrive or Google Drive.
A large building full of servers that store data and run online services.
Everyday objects with sensors and network connections that let them collect and share data over the internet.
An everyday device, such as a speaker, doorbell or thermostat, that connects to the internet and can be controlled remotely.
